The forecast uses the State Board of Elections’ mail-in figures through October 30, 2026, its unofficial early-voting counts through October 29, 2026 and its same-day registration counts through October 29, 2026. Every number on this page is read from the model’s committed outputs in data/turnout_model/. Ballots cast counts every ballot: election day, early voting, mail-in and provisional. A turnout rate is always ballots cast divided by a named denominator: active registration, eligible registration (active plus inactive registrants) or citizen voting-age population (CVAP).

The forecast in one table

The central forecast is 2,330,865 ballots cast, 54.2% of active registration. The range to quote runs from 2,060,722 to 2,553,256.

Statewide ballots cast and turnout rates. Active = active registration; eligible = active plus inactive registrants (projected for 2026); CVAP = citizen voting-age population (ACS).

Low assumes each party votes at its 2022 statewide level, a quiet midterm. High assumes each party votes at its 2018 level, an energized midterm. Central blends the two, party by party, with weights set by the written rule below. The intervals within each scenario are narrow by construction, because each draw is calibrated to a past election. They carry only cell-level noise and the shift in the 2026 electorate’s mix. The real uncertainty is the spread between low and high. That is why the headline range runs from low’s 5th percentile to high’s 95th. The 2022 rate on eligible divides by that election’s active plus inactive registrants, from the board’s inactive counts. No inactive counts exist for 2018, so its rate on eligible is not available. CVAP comes from a single ACS vintage matched to 2026, so it is not used for the past elections.

The 2026 forecasts include 7,142 ballots from same-day registration beyond 2022’s level, the same in every scenario; see Ballots already cast.

The 2026 rate on eligible is projected. There is no 2026 inactive count yet, so eligible is projected active registration times one plus the average of the 2022 and 2024 inactive-to-active ratios. The board’s own published 2026 percentage will use its actual eligible count and will differ.

What kind of model this is

The model treats each county and party group as a cell, 72 in all. In each cell, ballots cast are a binomial share of active registration. The model has three layers. Structure is estimated: how each cell’s turnout sits above or below its party’s statewide level in a midterm. Composition is computed: how the cell’s 2026 electorate differs in age and newness from 2022’s. Level is set by a written rule and bracketed between the 2022 and 2018 midterms.

The structure layer is a hierarchical binomial regression, fitted with lme4::glmer on 360 county x party rows from six elections (2018 and 2022 generals, 2022 and 2026 primaries, 2024 primary and general). It has a free statewide level for each election and party, four county census covariates, and random effects for county x party, county x election type and each observation. The formula, from fit_summary.json:

cbind(ballots_cast, active - ballots_cast) ~ 0 + ep + z_share_ba_plus + z_median_age + z_share_moved_past_year + z_share_owner_occupied + (1 | county:party_group) + (1 | county:election_type) + (1 | obs)
Variance components of the selected fit.
Random effect Variance (logit scale) Standard deviation
Observation (cell noise) 0.0144 0.120
County x election type 0.0048 0.070
County x party 0.0290 0.170

The full formula and the one without (1 | county:party_group:election_type) are singular: the county x party x type term is estimated at 0 (it is nearly the same as (1 | obs), with at most three rows per cell and election type), and (1 | county) is estimated at 0 once the covariates are in: the covariates and (1 | county:party_group) take up all county-level variation. Dropping (1 | county) as well leaves the estimates unchanged. zero_sd_terms in each attempt lists the terms at 0.

The level rule

The rule puts Democrats halfway between 2022 and 2018 (w = 0.5), Republicans halfway between 2022 and 2018 (w = 0.5) and Other (unaffiliated and minor parties) closer to 2018 (w = 0.7). The weight w is the share of the central level taken from 2018. The votes that moved it:

  • Democrats: registration momentum (2022-like) and ballots banked before election day (2018-like), so w = 0.5.
  • Republicans: primary participation (2022-like) and ballots banked before election day (2018-like), so w = 0.5.
  • Other (unaffiliated and minor parties): registration momentum (2018-like) and ballots banked before election day (2018-like), so w = 0.7.

The rule, verbatim from level_rule_text.csv:

Three scenarios per party p, on the logit scale, per draw k:
low: alpha = alpha*_{GG22,p,k}
high: alpha = alpha*_{GG18,p,k}
central: alpha = (1 - w_p) * alpha*_{GG22,p,k} + w_p * alpha*_{GG18,p,k}
w_p starts at 0.5 and moves by 0.1 per index vote, bounded to [0.2, 0.8].
Votes, per party p (DEM, REP, OTH), each in {-1, 0, +1} where +1 means 2018-like and -1 means 2022-like:
1. Registration momentum: position = (m26 - m22) / (m18 - m22) using indices.csv reg_momentum, reg_momentum_2022, reg_momentum_2018 (statewide row for p). Vote +1 if position >= 2/3, -1 if <= 1/3, else 0. If |m18 - m22| < 0.002 the analogues cannot discriminate: vote 0.
Amendment: a position outside [-0.5, 1.5] extrapolates beyond the two analogues and its sign is not interpretable: vote 0 when position < -0.5 or > 1.5; otherwise the thresholds above apply.
2. Mail requests, per registrant: project GG26 final sent for p as a linear trend over the available daily snapshots extended to 2026-10-27 (the request deadline; an assumption: no ballots are sent after it). Index = (projected GG26 final sent_p / 2026 projected active_p from denominators_gg26.csv) / (GG22 final sent_p (2022-11-28 file) / GG22 active_p from training.csv), so registration growth is not read as engagement. Vote +1 if >= 1.05, -1 if <= 0.95, else 0. (No 2018 analogue exists: 2018 predates the permanent mail-in list, so this index can only say "more or less engaged than 2022".)
3. Primary participation, per registrant: index = (GP26 ballots_p / GP26 active_p) / (GP22 ballots_p / GP22 active_p), from training.csv (DEM and REP; GP26 split estimated; OTH gets vote 0 because primaries are closed). Vote +1 if >= 1.05, -1 if <= 0.95, else 0.
Caveat: GP26 had an incumbent governor and GP22 an open seat, which depresses this index for reasons unrelated to November.
4. Ballots banked before election day, per registrant: banked = early-voting ballots (GG26: the board's unofficial eight-day county-by-party file at its latest as_of; GG22: the certified early-voting count in training.csv) plus mail ballots received back by the same number of days before election day (sent-returned county files; GG22 at the latest daily file on or before its election day minus that many days). Index = (GG26 banked_p / 2026 projected active_p) / (GG22 banked_p / GG22 active_p). Vote +1 if >= 1.05, -1 if <= 0.95, else 0.
Caveat: voters have been moving from election day to early voting and mail, so part of a high index is a change of habit rather than more voters; the vote is one step of 0.1, like the others. (No 2018 analogue: 2018 has no daily mail-return files and predates the permanent mail-in list.)
level_rule.csv also records the raw-count ratios (mail_count_ratio, primary_count_ratio, banked_count_ratio) beside the per-registrant indices that vote.

No 2018 analogue exists: 2018 predates the permanent mail-in list, so the mail index can only say more or less engaged than 2022. The rule’s GG26 projection is an OLS line of sent on calendar day over every daily snapshot, extended to 2026-10-27, the mail-in request deadline (assumed to be when sending stops), floored per county x party at the latest observed count. The mail vote depends on the projection choice: the sent series is step-like, so the all-snapshot slope is much steeper than the last few days’, and holding the latest count or extending the last three snapshots gives lower indices (see the _latest and _recent columns of level_rule.csv and the central_mail_latest and central_mail_recent scenarios). No GG22 trajectory of daily sent counts exists to anchor the choice. Once a snapshot dated on or after the deadline is in, every method uses the latest count, since sending is over, and the sensitivities equal the rule.

Caveats on the rule:

  • Mail has no 2018 analogue. 2018 came before the permanent mail-in list, so the mail index can only say whether voters are more or less engaged than in 2022.
  • Banked ballots mix engagement with habit. Voters have been moving from election day to early voting and mail. A voter who voted on election day in 2022 and early in 2026 raises the banked index without adding a ballot. The lowest party index is 1.17 against the 1.05 threshold, and the vote moves w by one step, like the others.
  • The 2026 primary had an incumbent governor; 2022’s was an open seat. That depresses the primary index for reasons unrelated to November. The 2026 primary’s party split is also an estimate from the voter file.
  • Momentum outside the analogue range votes 0. Registration momentum for Republicans (position 6.66) lies outside [-0.5, 1.5], beyond the range between 2022 and 2018, so the sign is not interpretable and it casts no vote.

Ballots already cast

Early voting ended on October 29. Voters cast 604,396 ballots in the eight days, by the board’s unofficial count, against 380,874 in 2022’s certified count, a rise of 59% on registration that grew 4%. By October 30, 2026, 4 days before the election, 376,967 mail ballots had come back, against 360,354 at the same point in 2022. The model uses these numbers in three places:

  • A fourth vote in the level rule. Early votes plus mail ballots back, per registrant, against 2022 at the same number of days out: every party is above 2022 by more than 5%, so every party gets a 2018-like vote (see the level rule above).
  • The mode split. Early voting is no longer a forecast: it is the count. Mail is the ballots received so far times 2022’s late-arrival multiplier, the certified vote-by-mail count over the ballots back 4 days before that election, 1.50 statewide. Election day is what is left.
  • A check on each scenario. 1,164,939 ballots are already banked or on their way: 604,396 early and 560,543 mail, projected. That leaves 3,136,595 active registrants who have not voted. Each scenario implies how many of them must vote on election day or provisionally. In 2022, 34.6% of the registrants who had not voted early or by mail turned out on election day; in 2018, 48.9%. The low scenario needs 29.9% of them, below 2022’s rate; central needs 37.2%, between 2022’s and 2018’s; high needs 43.0%, between 2022’s and 2018’s.
Ballots banked before election day and what each scenario needs on November 3 (early_vote_check.csv). 2026 early voting is the board’s unofficial count; 2026 mail is projected from ballots received so far. Registrants are active registration.

2026 central 2,330,865 604,396 560,543 50.0% 1,165,926 3,136,595 37.2%
2026 high 2,513,478 604,396 560,543 46.3% 1,348,539 3,136,595 43.0%

2022 actual 2,031,635 380,874 541,990 45.4% 1,108,771 3,201,292 34.6%

People who have already voted are the likeliest voters. With a larger share of registrants banked than in 2022, the ones left are, all else equal, less likely to vote than 2022’s were. That makes this check one-sided: a scenario that needs a higher rate than 2022’s from them is asking for more enthusiasm than in 2022, not just a change of habit. Read against that, the low scenario asks for less on election day than 2022 delivered (29.9% against 34.6%), from a pool that has already given up its likeliest voters to early voting and mail.

Same-day registration. During early voting, 3,802 people registered and voted at once, against 2,442 in 2022, and 3,562 registered voters updated their address and voted (1,730 in 2022). New registrants are not in the September-based 2026 registration, so they add ballots the cells cannot see. 2022’s same-day registrants are already in the reference levels, because certified ballots include them, so the model adds only 2026’s excess: election-day same-day registration is projected at 2022’s county counts (11,456 statewide) times the growth in early-voting same-day registration (1.56x), for 21,638 new registrants in all, against 14,496 for 2022 scaled to 2026 registration. The difference, 7,142 ballots, is added to every scenario. Address changes add nothing: those voters are already on the rolls.

Early voting is read from the board’s unofficial eight-day files (early-voting, county-party), which the State Board prints while the campaign runs; the certified early-voting count will differ slightly. Mail ballots received back are the sent-returned county files’ received measure (envelopes back, before the canvass accepts or rejects them). The 2022 comparison point is the GG22 daily file the same number of days before its election day (November 8, 2022), from the backfilled daily reports. The banked index treats early and mail ballots alike, so a voter who moved from election day to early voting since 2022 raises it without adding a ballot. Same-day registration adds voters who are not in the September-based 2026 active registration. The reference levels already carry the same-day registrants of their own year, because certified ballots cast include them, so the forecast adds only the excess of 2026’s same-day new registrants over GG22’s, scaled to 2026 registration: extra_c = sdr26_c - sdr22_c * active26_c / active22_c, where sdr22_c is GG22’s new registrants during early voting and on election day (same-day county file) and sdr26_c is GG26’s early-voting new registrants (latest same-day county file) plus GG22’s election-day new registrants in the county times the statewide growth of early-voting same-day registration from 2022 to 2026. Each county’s extra is split by party in proportion to GG26’s early-voting same-day new registrants (county-party file; the statewide party mix where a county has none) and added to every scenario as ballots with no noise: every same-day registrant votes. Address changes at the polls are voters already on the rolls and add nothing. GG22 serves as the same-day reference for all scenarios: 2018 allowed same-day registration only during early voting and its same-day files are not in the data. Rates on active keep the September-based denominator.

Counties

Central turnout rates on active registration run from 43.3% in Baltimore City to 65.4% in Talbot. In 23 of 24 counties the central rate lies between the county’s 2022 and 2018 rates. Relative to its forecast, the 90% interval is wider than the statewide one (3.5% of the forecast) in 24 of 24 counties, because cell noise averages out across the state.

Who votes: the electorate’s party mix

The forecast’s electorate is less Democratic than UMBC’s likely voters, with a larger share of other voters. In the central scenario, Democrats cast 53.9% of ballots, against 60% in UMBC’s sample. Other voters cast 19.9% of ballots in the central scenario, up from 16.0% in 2022. Their active registration has grown 20% since then, which drives the change.

Share of ballots cast by party group. Forecast and actual shares use registered party; the poll’s shares are as its release reports them.
Electorate Democrats Republicans Other (unaffiliated and minor)
2026 low 53.9% 27.6% 18.5%
2026 central 53.9% 26.2% 19.9%
2026 high 54.7% 25.5% 19.8%
2022 actual 55.9% 28.1% 16.0%
2018 actual 57.3% 27.4% 15.3%
UMBC Institute of Politics likely voters, September 22 to September 27, 2026 (n = 776, unweighted) 60% 25% 15%

The forecast’s party groups are registered party. A poll’s party shares come from its sample, which may record party as respondents describe it. Many unaffiliated registrants call themselves Democrats or Republicans when asked. Likely-voter screens also keep the respondents most certain to vote, and unaffiliated voters are the least likely to say so: UMBC’s own enthusiasm figures are lower for them. UMBC’s shares are unweighted by party, so they describe who answered, not the weighted estimate. The poll is a cross-check here and does not move the forecast.

Composition

Composition favours turnout in every cell, but the forecast uses it only to shift turnout between counties. Older electorates and fewer brand-new registrants raise each party’s expected 2026 rate. The statewide level of that boost cannot be trusted, so it is removed.

Every scenario uses comp_centred_cp = comp_cp minus the weighted mean over counties of comp for party p (weights: 2026 projected active registration, denominators_gg26.csv). composition_factors.csv’s comp is positive in every cell (statewide DEM +0.051, REP +0.080, OTH +0.034), but its statewide level is not identified: the 2022 mix comes from today’s voter file, which lacks the ~13% of the 2022 electorate who have since died or moved, and that bias is as large as the factor. Centred, composition only redistributes turnout across counties within a party and the level comes from the calibrated scenario. central_comp_level uses the uncentred comp with the central level; its statewide difference from central is the measure ballots_minus_central in forecast_statewide.csv. The midterm structure effect s_cp is treated as describing the 2022 composition, and comp is a change from it.

The factors are centred within party for one reason. The 2022 age mix comes from today’s voter file, which lacks the roughly 13% of the 2022 electorate who have since died or moved. That gap is as large as the factor itself, so its statewide level is not identified. Using the uncentred factor as a sensitivity adds +55,641 ballots to the central forecast, +1.3 points on the rate on active registration (55.5% against 54.2%).

How well the structure predicts a held-out midterm

Leaving out one midterm and predicting it from the other elections, the model beats a naive copy of the other midterm on 10 of 12 measures. Its county turnout rates on active registration miss by 2.2 points on average for 2022 and 2.2 for 2018. Both held-out tests calibrate statewide party totals to the actual result, so they test the county pattern, not the level.

The model loses to naive in 2 places:

  • Held-out 2022, county mean error in share of state ballots: model 0.17, naive 0.17 points.
  • Held-out 2018, county largest error in rate: model 8.08, naive 7.08 points. Both methods miss worst in Garrett.

How the votes will be cast

Mail ballots make up a smaller share of the forecast vote than in 2022, 24.0% against 26.7%. The largest mode is election day, at 46.9%.

Statewide ballots cast by mode, central scenario (mode_split.csv).

Total 2,330,865 100.0% 100.0%

Early voting is the board’s unofficial count, 604,396 statewide; early voting is over. Mail ballots are the 376,967 received by October 30, 2026 times 2022’s late-arrival multiplier in each county (certified vote-by-mail over the ballots back the same number of days before that election), capped at the ballots sent. That is 560,543 mail ballots, 85.6% of the 654,876 sent. Provisional ballots keep their 2022 share of each county’s vote, and election day is the rest. No county hit the cap of 90% of its ballots by mail.

What this cannot see

  • Election-day weather. Rain or snow on November 3 would cut election-day voting, forecast at 46.9% of ballots cast.
  • Late changes in the races. The governor’s race polls at Moore +27 (UMBC). A tightening race, or a hot down-ballot contest, could lift turnout above the rule’s blend.
  • Changes to mail voting. A court ruling, or a change to a deadline for mail ballots, would break the mail projection, which assumes late ballots arrive as they did in 2022.
  • Election-day same-day registration. It is projected from 2022’s county counts and the growth in early-voting same-day registration. Other registration after September is not modelled: the denominators come from September 2026 active registration.
  • The early-vote count is unofficial. The certified early-voting count will differ slightly.
  • Survivor bias in composition. The 2022 age mix is built from today’s voter file, which lacks people who died or moved since 2022.
  • The 2026 primary’s party split is estimated. The board has not yet published 2026 primary turnout by party, so the split comes from the voter file.
  • The 2014 general is left out. The structure rests on 2018 and later elections.
  • Two different denominators. The board’s 2018 to 2024 turnout sheets divide by active registration. Its 2026 guide divides by all eligible voters, active plus inactive. This report shows both.

Data and reproducibility

Run the whole model and this report from the repo root, after make build-db:

make turnout-model

The scripts use the renv project in scripts/turnout_model/ (renv.lock); see scripts/turnout_model/README.md. The forecast reads the board’s mail-in files through October 30, 2026 and its early-voting and same-day files through October 29, 2026. Every input and output has a provenance file:
